facts.statement: Parahelicoprion lived during the Early Permian.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Early Permian

facts.statement: The genus Parahelicoprion was formally described by Karpinsky in 1924.
facts.quote: authority: Karpinsky, 1924

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Parahelicoprion is Helicoprion clerci.
facts.quote: type_species: Helicoprion clerci

facts.statement: Parahelicoprion mariosuarezi was described by Merino-Rodo and Janvier in 1986.
facts.quote: subdivision: *P. mariosuarezi Merino-Rodo & Janvier, 1986

facts.statement: Xystracanthus grandis and Physonemus mirabilis have been suggested as potential synonyms for Parahelicoprion.
facts.quote: synonyms: *Helicoprion? (Karpinsky, 1899) Xystracanthus grandis? (Moore, 1929) Physonemus mirabilis? (St. John & Worthen, 1875)

facts.statement: The genus Parahelicoprion contains two species: P. clerci from Russia and P. mariosuarezi from Bolivia.
facts.quote: The genus contains two species: P. clerci from the Arta Beds of the Ural Mountains of Russia, and P. mariosuarezi from the Copacabana Formation of Bolivia.

facts.statement: Parahelicoprion belongs to the family Helicoprionidae within the order Eugeneodontiformes.
facts.quote: The characteristics of this whorl are unique to fishes of the order Eugeneodontiformes, and more specifically the family Helicoprionidae to which Parahelicoprion belongs.

facts.statement: The holotype of P. clerci consists of tooth fragments that were damaged by mining and broken into pieces.
facts.quote: The holotype of Parahelicoprion clerci, which consists only of tooth fragments, was badly damaged by mining and is broken into several pieces.

facts.statement: The holotype of P. mariosuarezi consists of nine partial teeth with broken outer edges.
facts.quote: That of the Bolivian P. mariosuarezi consists of nine partial teeth, the outer edges of which are broken off.

facts.statement: Due to incomplete fossils, estimates of Parahelicoprion's size and ecology are speculative, though it is assumed to have been large, predatory, and potentially pelagic.
facts.quote: Estimates of the extent of the complete whorl, body size, and ecology of Parahelicoprion are speculative as a result of its incomplete fossils, although it is assumed to have been very large, predatory, and potentially pelagic.

facts.statement: The type specimen of P. clerci was found in the Ural Mountains of Russia in Artinskian strata.
facts.quote: The type specimen of Parahelicoprion clerci was found in the Ural Mountains region of Russia, in strata dated to the Artinskian stage of the Cisuralian (early Permian) epoch.

facts.statement: The first portions of the P. clerci specimen were discovered incidentally by a miner and damaged during collection.
facts.quote: The first five portions of the specimen to be found, which consist of several teeth, were discovered incidentally by a miner and were badly damaged as a result poor handling during collection.

facts.statement: P. mariosuarezi was described by Merino-Roda and Janvier in 1986.
facts.quote: A second species, Parahelicoprion mariosuarezi, was described and tentatively assigned to the genus in 1986 by Dagmar Merino-Roda and Philippe Janvier.

facts.statement: P. mariosuarezi was discovered in the Copacabana Formation of Bolivia and dated to the Asselian stage.
facts.quote: This species, which is also based only on its type specimen (designated no. 6097, YPFB), was discovered in the Copacabana Formation of Yaurichambi, Bolivia, and was dated to the Asselian stage of the early Permian.

facts.statement: The holotype of P. mariosuarezi was found preserved in calcarious red sandstone.
facts.quote: The holotype, a partial set of teeth, was found preserved in a layer of calcarious red sandstone.

facts.statement: P. mariosuarezi is named in honor of Dr. Mario Suarez-Riglos, and its type specimen is housed at the Noel Kempff Mercado Natural History Museum.
facts.quote: The species is named in honor of Dr. Mario Suarez-Riglos, and the type specimen is currently housed in the collection of the Noel Kempff Mercado Natural History Museum.

facts.statement: P. clerci was initially named Helicoprion clerci by Alexander Karpinsky in 1916.
facts.quote: The type specimen of Parahelicoprion was initially named Helicoprion clerci by the Russian geologist Alexander Karpinsky in 1916.

facts.statement: Karpinsky reassigned H. clerci to the genus Parahelicoprion in 1924.
facts.quote: Karpinsky reassigned Helicoprion clerci to its own genus in a work published in 1924

facts.statement: Onésime Clerc brought the holotype of P. clerci to Karpinsky's attention.
facts.quote: Clerc was responsible for bringing the holotype specimen of P. clerci to Karpinsky's attention.

facts.statement: Both species of Parahelicoprion share tooth crowns with long, backwards-sweeping recessed lower sections and curved denticles along their edges.
facts.quote: While some authors have suggested the genus lacks defining, autapomorphous features, the tooth crowns of both species of Parahelicoprion are noted to share extremely long, backwards-sweeping, recessed lower sections (referred to as "wings" or "ribs" by researchers) which extend nearly to the base of the tooth root, as well as curved denticles or serrations along the edges of these sections.

facts.statement: Authors have suggested P. mariosuarezi had a short tooth whorl at the tip of elongated jaws, but acknowledged the material is too fragmentary for confident comparison.
facts.quote: Various other authors have agreed with a Sarcoprion-like interpretation, but have acknowledged that the shape of the complete whorl is not known and that the material is too fragmentary for such comparisons to be confidently made.

facts.statement: Researchers debate whether large fin spines found with Parahelicoprion correspond to edestoids, copulatory organs of symmoriiform fishes, or holocephalans.
facts.quote: In a 2018 publication, researcher Serge Naugholnykh asserted personal belief that these spines correspond to edestoids, although sickle-like spine fossils are believed by other researchers to represent the copulatory organs of symmoriiform fishes or, alternatively, of holocephalans.

facts.statement: The holotype of Parahelicoprion clerci was prepared and assembled by Karpinsky in 1916.
facts.quote: During preparation by Karpinsky in 1916, three of these fragments were glued together in order to reflect their in-life articulation

facts.statement: The holotype of Parahelicoprion clerci measures 25 cm (10 inches) in profile and includes six articulated tooth crowns plus a smaller fragment.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen as recognized today spans 25 cm (10 in) in profile view and consists of six articulated tooth crowns, as well as an associated smaller tooth fragment.

facts.statement: The upper tips of Parahelicoprion tooth crowns are uniquely rounded and blunt, unlike the pointed tips of many related edestoids.
facts.quote: The upper tips of all the known tooth crowns are uniquely rounded and blunt, rather than tapering to a point like those of many other related edestoids.

facts.statement: The form of the serrations and crenulations on Parahelicoprion teeth is unique to this species.
facts.quote: The form of these serrations and crenulations is unique to this species.

facts.statement: The base of Parahelicoprion's tooth whorl is entirely fused with no gaps between segments.
facts.quote: The base (or root) of Parahelicoprion's whorl is described as entirely fused, with no gaps or separations between segments forming separate teeth.

facts.statement: The interior of Parahelicoprion teeth is well-preserved and composed of vasodentin, a spongy dentin form common in fishes.
facts.quote: The interior of the teeth remains well-preserved, and was composed of a spongy form of dentin identified by Karpinsky as vasodentin (a form common among fishes).

facts.statement: Parahelicoprion mariosuarezi preserves a denticle-bearing parasymphyseal tooth near the midline of the mouth, a type not found in P. clerci.
facts.quote: This species also preserves a single denticle-bearing parasymphyseal tooth (a paired tooth near the midline of the mouth) along the edge of the whorl, a tooth type which is not known from P. clerci.

facts.statement: Parahelicoprion teeth increase significantly in size toward the rear of the whorl.
facts.quote: The teeth increase significantly in size towards the rear of the whorl, with the largest tooth crown tip (not including the serrated "rib") of the holotype measuring 3.4 cm in height, 3 cm across, and 1.9 cm wide at the widest point

facts.statement: Parahelicoprion teeth farthest forward are rounder and more asymmetrical than the nearly symmetrical rear teeth.
facts.quote: The teeth farthest forward being rounder and more asymmetrical than those at the back, which are nearly completely symmetrical in profile.

facts.statement: The rear edges of the frontmost tooth crowns in Parahelicoprion form sharp, non-serrated cutting blades.
facts.quote: The rear edges of the frontmost crown's tips thin to form sharp cutting blades, which are not serrated.

facts.statement: In the rear tooth crowns of Parahelicoprion, both the front and rear edges are blade-like.
facts.quote: In the rear crown tips, both the front and rear edges of the tooth are blade-like.

facts.statement: Like other family members, the teeth of Parahelicoprion angle forward in the mouth.
facts.quote: As in other members of its family, the teeth of the whorl angle forward in the mouth.

facts.statement: The outer coating of Parahelicoprion teeth is debated; Karpinsky called it enamel, but it may be enameloid (vitrodentine) like in other helicoprionids.
facts.quote: The outer coating of the teeth, which is described by Karpinsky as being enamel, has been abraded away across most of the tooth fragments. This substance has alternatively been identified as enameloid (also called vitrodentine) in other helicoprionids and other fishes, rather than true enamel.

facts.statement: Unlike other eugeneodonts, trabecular dentin was likely absent from Parahelicoprion teeth.
facts.quote: Unlike other eugeneodonts, trabecular dentin (a porous form found in cartilaginous fish) was likely absent from the teeth.

facts.statement: The outer cutting edges of P. mariosuarezi teeth are thought to be similar to P. clerci based on crown shape and thickness.
facts.quote: Despite being unpreserved, the outer cutting edges of the teeth in P. mariosuarezi are thought to have been similar to P. clerci, due to the preserved portions of the crowns being similar in shape and thickness.

facts.statement: The rear portion of the whorl in Parahelicoprion mariosuarezi is described as fused.
facts.quote: The rear portion of the whorl is described as being fused.

facts.statement: Karpinsky suggested Parahelicoprion clerci was very large to accommodate its significantly larger tooth crowns compared to Helicoprion.
facts.quote: Karpinsky himself did not provide body length estimates in his descriptions, but did note that the tooth crowns of Parahelicoprion clerci were significantly larger than those of any then-known Helicoprion specimens and suggested that the animal must have been very large to accommodate them.

facts.statement: Richard Ellis estimated Parahelicoprion was at least 100 feet long, unless it had a gigantic head or oversized teeth.
facts.quote: Ellis states that, in spite of the fragmentary nature of the known material, "... unless it [Parahelicoprion] was an animal with a gigantic head or outlandishly oversized teeth, it had to have been a monster, at least 100 feet long and maybe more."

facts.statement: Non-academic sources suggest Parahelicoprion lengths of 11-13 meters, but these are not supported by scientific literature.
facts.quote: Lengths of 11-13 meters have more recently been suggested for Parahelicoprion by online sources, although these numbers originate from non-academic amateur researchers and are not supported by scientific literature.

facts.statement: It is debated whether crushing teeth similar to Campodus or Orodus were present in Parahelicoprion, as no other teeth are confidently associated with the species.
facts.quote: No other teeth are confidently associated with this species, although crushing teeth similar to those of Campodus or Orodus may have been present.

facts.statement: Karpinsky considered it likely that parts of the Parahelicoprion holotype were destroyed by mining or never collected.
facts.quote: The surface texture of the teeth has been badly damaged by mining, and Karpinsky considered it likely that parts of the fossil had been destroyed or never collected.

facts.statement: Estimates of Parahelicoprion's total body size are controversial despite its large tooth crowns.
facts.quote: While the known tooth crowns of the genus are considered to be among the largest of the eugeneodonts, estimates of Parahelicoprion's total body size have been considered controversial.

facts.statement: Some researchers consider it unreasonable to give precise total length estimates for Parahelicoprion due to fragmentary fossil material.
facts.quote: Due to the fragmentary nature of the known material, it has been considered unreasonable by some researchers to give precise total length estimates for Helicoprion, Parahelicoprion, or any other members of Edestoidea.

facts.statement: The family Helicoprionidae is defined by possessing tooth whorls with forward-angled, blade-like tooth crowns and often completely fused tooth roots.
facts.quote: The helicoprionids (also called agassizodontids by some authors) are defined by possessing tooth whorls with forward angled, blade-like tooth crowns and, in many genera, tooth roots which are completely fused.

facts.statement: In 2018, Serge Naugholnykh proposed that Parahelicoprion clerci is synonymous with Helicoprion, representing an especially large individual of that genus.
facts.quote: In a 2018 paper, paleontologist Serge Naugholnykh proposed that P. clerci simply represents an especially large individual of Helicoprion and that the two genera are synonymous

facts.statement: The genus Parahelicoprion was named by Karpinsky in 1924.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Karpinsky, 1924

facts.statement: The genus Parahelicoprion includes two species: P. clerci and P. mariosuarezi.
facts.quote: subdivision: P. clerci (Karpinsky, 1916) P. mariosuarezi Merino-Rodo & Janvier, 1986

facts.statement: Parahelicoprion was a carnivore that lived in marine environments.
facts.quote: Parahelicoprion was a carnivore that inhabited marine environments.

facts.statement: It has been suggested that Parahelicoprion was the apex predator of its ecosystem, with its serrated tooth whorl adapted for cutting prey.
facts.quote: It has been suggested to have been the apex predator of its ecosystem, with the serrated tooth whorl being adapted for cutting prey.

facts.statement: It is hypothesized that members of the Helicoprionidae were molluscivorous, feeding primarily on ammonoid and coleoid cephalopods.
facts.quote: it has been hypothesized that members of the Helicoprionidae were molluscivorous and fed primarily on ammonoid and coleoid cephalopods

facts.statement: Parahelicoprion fossils from the Copacabana Formation date to the boundary between the Carboniferous and Permian periods.
facts.quote: The Copacabana Formation represented a shallow marine habitat, somewhat older than the Arta Beds and dated to the boundary between the Carboniferous and the Permian.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that the layer preserving Parahelicoprion in the Copacabana Formation formed in a shallow, intertidal habitat.
facts.quote: Merino-Rodo and Janvier suggest that the sandstones which compose the upper fish-bearing layer and which preserve the whorl of Parahelicoprion may have formed in an even shallower, intertidal habitat

facts.statement: The age of the Copacabana Formation was determined using conodont index fossils.
facts.quote: it is from these index fossils that the age of the formation has been determined.

facts.statement: The latest known occurrence of Parahelicoprion is the Artinskian stage of the Permian, and it is assumed to have gone extinct by the end of the Cisuralian.
facts.quote: The latest known occurrence of the genus is the Artinskian stage of the Permian, and it is assumed to have been extinct by the end of the Cisuralian.

facts.statement: Karpinsky suggested that the extinction of Uralian edestoids like Parahelicoprion was caused by the disappearance of the seaway connecting the Arctic and Tethys oceans.
facts.quote: Karpinsky has suggested that the disappearance of the seaway connecting the Arctic and Tethys oceans was directly responsible for the extinction of the Uralian edestoids.

facts.statement: Karpinsky suggested that the large size and specialized dentition of Parahelicoprion made it difficult to adapt to environmental changes.
facts.quote: he does suggests that the large size and extremely specialized dentition of the genus made it difficult for it to adapt to environmental change.

facts.statement: Fossilized teeth of Parahelicoprion from the Divya Formation show no post-mortem wear, indicating they lived in calm waters.
facts.quote: Fossilized teeth collected from the Divya Formation show no indication of post-mortem wear, indicating calm waters.

facts.statement: Parahelicoprion lived between 298.9 and 293.52 million years ago during the Asselian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Asselian to Asselian (298.9 to 293.52 million years ago)
